md:
### Constriction against restrictive cardiomyopathy at a glance

| Feature | Constrictive pericarditis | Restrictive cardiomyopathy |
|---|---|---|
| Causes | Idiopathic, previous cardiac surgery, mediastinal radiotherapy; tuberculosis elsewhere | Amyloid, sarcoid, haemochromatosis, radiation |
| Mitral annular e′ | Preserved; medial e′ exceeds lateral ("annulus reversus") in 75%; with heart failure, e′ over 8 cm/s points to constriction | Reduced, 6 cm/s or less |
| Mitral inflow | Restrictive pattern (E/A over 2, DT under 160) | Restrictive pattern (E/A over 2, DT under 160) |
| Respiratory variation | Mitral E over 25%, tricuspid E over 40%; septal bounce or shift; hepatic vein expiratory reversal | — |
| Ventricular interdependence (FRCS Atlas, unchecked) | Enhanced: RV and LV systolic pressures move in opposite directions with respiration | RV and LV systolic pressures move together |
| Catheter | Equal end-diastolic pressures; RV end-diastolic over one third of RV systolic (95% sensitive); square root sign; prominent y descent | — |
| Pericardium | Thickened (MRI better than CT), but normal thickness in up to 20%; calcified on the film in 40% | — |
| Treatment | Anti-inflammatory trial if inflamed (CMR oedema or LGE with raised CRP); radical pericardiectomy for permanent constriction | — |

Source: summarised from this tab (TSRA Review ch. 48 and 86; ESC 2025 myocarditis and pericarditis guideline; the interdependence row is from the FRCS Atlas draft, not checked).
anchor: The alternative diagnosis is restrictive cardiomyopathy (amyloid, sarcoid, haemochromatosis, radiation).

md:
### Surgery for tricuspid endocarditis in people who inject drugs: what each source says

| Option | Luc et al. 2019 (meta-analysis) | AHA 2022 statement | de Waha et al. 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Repair | Preferred, but extensive destruction often precludes it | Repair and avoid prosthetic material where possible; repair a regurgitant valve as well as removing vegetations | Preferred when feasible: lower reinfection, no prosthetic material |
| Replacement | 86% of 752 patients; 30-day mortality 7%, recurrent endocarditis 19% | Reasonable when repair is not possible; recurrent prosthetic endocarditis a particular concern | Bioprosthesis often chosen; no difference in reinfection between mechanical and biological among PWID; epicardial pacing lead |
| Valvectomy | Acceptable initial therapy, a bridge to staged replacement; 30-day mortality 13%, right heart failure 27% | Not recommended: can cause significant morbidity | Selected patients with ongoing injecting; a stabilising first stage before staged replacement |
| Percutaneous aspiration | AngioVac reported as promising | Alternative to prevent further septic emboli; does not treat valve dysfunction | Adjunct for large vegetations, recurrent emboli or instability in poor surgical candidates; evidence limited |
| Addiction care | Team including addiction services; medication-assisted treatment, harm reduction, naloxone | A further operation needs an addiction treatment plan supported by addiction-trained clinicians | Start buprenorphine or methadone in hospital; Endocarditis Team with addiction medicine |

Source: summarised from the Luc 2019, AHA scientific statements and de Waha 2026 sections of this tab.
anchor: Acute specialties dominate in hospital; addiction care determines long-term outcome.

md:
### ANOCA and INOCA endotypes at a glance

| Endotype | What defines it | Treatment (ESC 2024) |
|---|---|---|
| Endothelial dysfunction | Abnormal response to intracoronary acetylcholine (80% of those tested in ILIAS) | Statin and ACE inhibitor; ACE inhibitor for symptoms (IIa B) |
| Microvascular angina, impaired vasodilation | CFR under 2.5, or IMR 25 or more (HMR over 2.5, MRR under 2.7) | Beta-blocker, CCB, ranolazine, trimetazidine, ivabradine; antianginals against demand ischaemia (IIa B) |
| Microvascular vasospasm | Symptoms and ECG changes on acetylcholine with under 90% lumen reduction | CCB, second CCB, nitrates |
| Epicardial vasospasm | Symptoms, ischaemic ECG changes and 90% or more lumen reduction | CCB (I A), nitrates (IIa B), nicorandil; severe: high-dose diltiazem |
| Overlapping endotypes | Combinations of the above | Nitrates, CCBs and other vasodilators combined (IIb B) |

Source: summarised from the ESC 2024 chronic coronary syndromes ANOCA/INOCA section (section 5.2, Recommendation Table 25).

md:
### Exercise prescription by FITT (ESC 2024)

| | Aerobic | Resistance |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency | At least 3 days a week, preferably 6 to 7 | At least 2 days a week |
| Intensity | Moderate or moderate-to-high, set from the individual's peak (% VO2 max, % peak heart rate or ventilatory thresholds) | Printed as "6%–80%" of one-repetition maximum (probably a typesetting error) |
| Time | 150 to 300 min a week moderate, or 75 to 150 min vigorous (I B) | 1 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions |
| Type | Moderate continuous training; high-intensity intervals only for selected targets such as peak VO2 | 8 to 10 exercises covering the major muscle groups |

Source: summarised from the 2024 ESC chronic coronary syndromes guideline, section 4.1.3 and Recommendation Table 15, as given in this section.
anchor: Continued exercise (phase III rehabilitation) is recommended.
